summary: This RFC suggests a simple way for workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server. It revises RFC 918 and is Post Office Protocol version 2. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: POP2 lets a workstation read messages stored on a mailbox server. The client retrieves each message and tells the server whether it was received and should be kept or deleted.

questions: what is the difference between acks and ackd
subtitle: An early protocol for a workstation to retrieve mail from a mailbox server.

tldr.problem: A workstation may be unavailable when mail arrives, so users need to retrieve mail from a mailbox kept on an always-up server.
tldr.mechanism: POP2 uses commands over a reliable stream. A client logs in, selects a mailbox, reads a message, retrieves it, and acknowledges whether to keep, delete, or retry it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 937 is Historic and obsoletes RFC 918. The server keeps no record of which messages were retrieved in earlier sessions.

today: RFC 937 has Historic status and obsoletes RFC 918. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What POP2 Does
sections.content:
The Post Office Protocol Version 2 (POP2) lets a user's workstation access mail held on a mailbox server. The RFC expects mail to be sent to that server using SMTP; the workstation is a way to view and retrieve the messages.

POP2 uses a reliable data stream such as TCP. When using TCP, the server listens on port 109. The RFC describes POP2 as a proposed protocol for the ARPA-Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: POP2 lets a workstation retrieve mail from a separate mailbox server. The workstation does not need to be the host that receives mail.

sections.title: A Mailbox on an Always-Available Host
sections.content:
The RFC assumes the user's mailbox lives on a server that is expected to be available, while a workstation may be powered down or unavailable as a mail server. A user can therefore access the mailbox from different workstations without changing the mailbox address.

POP2 is deliberately simple and transmits whole messages without parsing their headers. If something goes wrong, its basic rule is to close the connection; it is not a user interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The mailbox stays on a server while the user's workstation may be offline. POP2 transfers complete messages and leaves their interpretation to the mail program.

sections.title: The Message Reading Cycle
sections.content:
The server opens with a greeting. The client sends HELO with a user name and password, then receives the mailbox message count. It can choose a mailbox with FOLD, request a message with READ, and retrieve it with RETR.

After retrieval, the client sends one acknowledgement. ACKS keeps the message, ACKD marks it for deletion, and NACK says to keep it because it was not received. Deletion takes effect when the mailbox is released or another mailbox is selected.
sections.plainLanguage: The client logs in, selects a mailbox, and requests a message. After receiving it, the client tells the server whether to keep it, mark it for deletion, or leave it for another attempt.

sections.title: Replies, Message Length and Limits
sections.content:
Commands and replies end with carriage return and line feed. A reply begins with a plus sign for success, a minus sign for failure, an equals sign for a message length, or a number sign for a mailbox count. Message lengths count characters, including the two-character line ending.

The RFC sets a maximum command line and reply line length of 512 characters and a maximum text line length of 1000 characters. It also specifies timeouts so neither side waits forever for a response or a next command.
sections.plainLanguage: The first character of a reply tells the client whether it is a success, failure, length, or message count. The RFC also limits line lengths and requires timeouts.

sections.title: Session State and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC gives client and server state diagrams that describe which command or reply can come next. Unexpected input is treated as an error; the client quits, and the server sends an error and closes the connection.

The server keeps no state from one session to another, so it cannot identify messages received since the user's last session. The only access control described is the user name and password supplied in HELO.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server follow a defined sequence of states. The server does not remember earlier sessions, so it cannot identify only newly arrived mail.
